views.title: The Roth IRA, the checking account and the car are in Jordan’s name alone, and no one is named to get them.
views.subtitle: Everything else is joint with Casey or has Casey’s name on a form. There is no will and no trust, so those three things would go to a court first, and Colorado’s default list would decide who gets them.

notes.title: Neither Jordan nor Casey has a will.
notes.body: The intake notes say so (p. 1). Without one, anything that ends up in court goes to whoever Colorado’s default list names, in shares the state sets. With a six-year-old, a will is also where a guardian for Mia is named.

notes.title: The Roth IRA has no one named to get it.
notes.body: Roth IRA statement, p. 2: no beneficiary on file. Jordan can log in to Summit and name Casey, with Mia as backup. Ten minutes.

notes.title: The checking account is in Jordan’s name alone.
notes.body: Checking statement, p. 1: one name, no one listed to get it. Casey couldn’t use it until a court acted. The bank can add Casey as payable-on-death or put both names on it.

notes.title: The car is titled to Jordan alone.
notes.body: Car title, p. 1: one owner, no co-owner. Colorado may have a shortcut for vehicles; this page didn’t check. Adding Casey to the title is the usual fix.

notes.title: The 401(k) names Casey, with no backup.
notes.body: 401(k) statement, p. 2: Casey first, no one after. That works as long as Casey is living. Adding Mia as backup, through a trust or a custodian the attorney sets up, closes the gap.

notes.title: Casey’s 403(b) names Jordan, with no backup.
notes.body: 403(b) statement, p. 2. If Jordan died first, Casey would need to update it. Adding a backup now avoids that.

notes.title: Mia, age 6, is the backup on the $750K policy.
notes.body: Policy, p. 3: Casey first, then Mia. If it ever went to Mia while she is a minor, the money would need a court-appointed guardian or a custodian. The attorney can say whether a trust for Mia should be named instead.

views.kicker: If you have beneficiary forms and joint accounts but no will
views.law: Who owns what, as the deed, the title and the account records show it. In Colorado, what is in one spouse’s name is that spouse’s.

views.title: If Jordan dies, $1.41M goes straight to Casey, and $131K gets stuck in court with no will to say who gets it.
views.subtitle: How each thing in Jordan’s name would get to someone if Jordan died and Casey survived. Probate is the court process that sorts out what a person held in their own name with no form or co-owner. With no will, the state’s default list decides who receives it.

notes.title: The Roth IRA is the biggest thing that would get stuck.
notes.body: No one is named on it (Roth IRA statement, p. 2), so the brokerage would pay it to Jordan’s estate, which is the pile of things a court sorts out. Until the court picks someone to be in charge, probably Casey, no one can touch the $89K, and money paid to an estate usually has to come out faster, with more tax. Naming Casey on the form fixes all of that.

notes.title: The everyday account would be frozen until a court acts.
notes.body: It is only in Jordan’s name and no one is listed to get it (checking statement, p. 1). Adding Casey as payable-on-death at the bank, or putting both names on the account, keeps it out of court.

notes.title: The car would wait too, unless Colorado has a shortcut.
notes.body: The title is in Jordan’s name alone (car title, p. 1). Colorado has simpler procedures for vehicles and small estates; this page didn’t check whether one applies. Adding Casey to the title is the usual fix.

notes.title: With no will, the state decides, and Mia’s share would be tied up.
notes.body: Colorado’s default list usually splits what is left between the spouse and the children. Mia is six, so her part would sit in a court-supervised account until she is an adult. A will makes all of this a non-question, and it is also where someone is named to take care of Mia.

notes.title: Casey’s own 403(b) still names Jordan.
notes.body: It names Jordan with no backup (403(b) statement, p. 2). If Jordan died, Casey would need to name someone new, and a will is where a backup for Mia gets named too.

fixes.roth: Jordan logs in to Summit and names Casey, with Mia as backup. Ten minutes.
fixes.checking: At the bank, add Casey as payable-on-death, or add Casey to the account.
fixes.car: Add Casey to the title, or ask the county office whether a simpler transfer applies.
fixes.casey: Casey logs in to the Denver Public Schools plan and adds a backup after Jordan. Ten minutes.

views.kicker: If you have beneficiary forms and joint accounts but no will
views.law: How things pass at a death: joint accounts to the other owner, accounts with a named person to that person, and the rest through probate court. With no will, Colorado’s intestate succession rules (Colorado Revised Statutes title 15, article 11, part 1).
